title: What Will Not Wash Away
logline: A rock a little over two hundred metres high stands out of the southern lowlands with cave temples cut and painted on terraces up its side, and in one of those caves the island's entire recorded history lay on palm leaves through two hundred monsoons, readable at the end of it only because somebody had kept a second, plainer text beside it.
human_question: If the only way I can follow something is a plainer version of it, is the plainer version a compromise, or is it the point?

place.what_kind_of_place: A single granite mass rising a little over two hundred metres straight out of flat lowland country a short way in from the sea, with four smaller rocks standing around it. It is not a citadel and nothing was ever fortified on it: it is a working monastery, occupied more or less continuously for over two thousand years, arranged as a series of stepped terraces up one flank. Seven cave temples are cut back under the rock's overhangs across five of those terraces, each cave with a groove chiselled along the brow of the rock above its mouth so that rain runs off and drips clear instead of into the cave. The climb is a stone stair of a few hundred steps taken up through a natural cleft in the rock under very old trees. Inside the caves are reclining figures up to fourteen or fifteen metres long, walls painted floor to ceiling in layers laid one over another across three or four centuries, and short inscriptions cut into the rock itself, the earliest of them older than the paintings by roughly two thousand years. On the top terrace there is a stupa, a bo tree and open sky in every direction. Monks live and work here and people come up to worship, which sets the terms for everything the film can do.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off. First, the rock itself at first light, out of level paddy and coconut, one mass with four lesser rocks around it and mist still lying in the low ground, which from the air reads as a thing that arrived rather than a thing that grew. Second, the terraces in raked side light: cave mouths stacked one above another up a vertical face, a stone stair disappearing into a cleft, enormous roots over the steps, and along the brow of every overhang a shallow man-cut channel following the rock's own curve. Third, and this is the shot the film exists for, the weather: rain coming in off the sea across open country, and then a curtain of water pouring off the lip of an overhang in front of a cave mouth while the cave behind it stays completely dry and completely dark. Then the summit standing above the rain with the sea on one side and forested mountains on the other.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Water and light, and neither is anyone's to arrange. A shower builds, arrives, pours off the brows of the caves for a few minutes and is gone, and where it goes is down the face and off the rock. Light moves up the terraces in the morning and off them in the evening, and reaches only a metre or two into any of the caves, so the paintings are lit for a short part of the day and then are not. The trees over the stair move in wind that the terraces below do not feel. Over much longer time the paintings themselves are going: they were painted over older paintings, and they are flaking in the damp, which is visible in frame and needs no commentary.
place.when_it_looks_best: Early morning for the rock out of the lowland mist and for light entering the lower caves, late afternoon for raked light across the terraces, and the summit at either end of the day. The film also needs rain, which means the wet windows on this coast rather than the dry ones: broadly the second inter-monsoon in October and November, and again around the onset of the south-west monsoon in May. A showery day is worth more to this film than a clear one, and the two can usually be had in the same week.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a rock and what has been kept dry inside it. It has its own shape: flat country, then one rock, then a stair into a cleft, then terrace after terrace of painted caves going up, then weather arriving and pouring off the stone, and then the top, above the rain, with the sea one way and the mountains the other. A viewer who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete climb, some of the best painted interiors in the south of the island, one extraordinary weather shot, and the plain physical fact of a groove cut in rock two thousand years ago that is still doing its job.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes an argument about two levels of speech. The voice never contradicts what is on screen and never adjudicates anything: it points out that everything on this rock exists in two registers at once. A stair cut so that the terraces can be reached. A groove cut so that what is inside stays legible. Painted walls that tell the hard part of a teaching in everyday pictures. And, recorded here in 1826, a prose commentary kept beside a verse chronicle for the sole reason that without it the verse could not be read. The film's claim is the sources' own: the plainer level was chosen on purpose so that people could follow, and it is not a lesser thing for being plain. The last beat then refuses the ending that would be easy, because these books do not say the final truth is reached by reading better.

sequence.on_screen: First light from the air, high and moving in slowly. Level lowland country, paddy and coconut, mist in the low ground, and out of the middle of it one rock, with four smaller rocks standing off it.
sequence.voice: When these books want an example of an ordinary word, the word they reach for is this one. A being, a person, a tree, a mountain, a river. Those are the names the teaching was given in, and the reason given is not a grand one: so that whoever was listening could follow it easily.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level at the foot of the rock, then the stair: a few hundred stone steps going up through a natural cleft, roots of very old trees crossing them, the light dropping as the walls close in.
sequence.voice: In 1826 a British civil servant obtained, from the library of the monastery on this rock, palm-leaf copies of a prose commentary on the Mahāvaṃsa. The chronicle's verse had been effectively unreadable. A monk here told him a key existed, and he wrote that fitted into the verse it reduced the whole thing to a commonsense narrative. Eleven years later the first English translation was published, and with it the island's recoverable chronology. What kind of transaction that was is still argued over. What is not argued over is that the chronicle was only legible because a plainer text had been kept beside it.

sequence.on_screen: The terraces from the air, tight in and looking along the face rather than down: five stacked levels on one rock, cave mouths on each, low sun raking across them.
sequence.voice: These compendiums sort everything there is into heaps. That is the word, and it was chosen deliberately: the same term in the language has grander senses, virtue, a tree trunk, and the commentators set every one of them aside and keep only heap, collection, portion. A plain word, doing plain work. What the sorting is for is stated as plainly: not to tidy the world up, but to loosen the habit of saying mine about each part of it.

sequence.on_screen: One cave mouth in full, from the terrace outside it. The overhang above, and along the brow of the overhang a shallow channel cut by hand, following the curve of the rock for the whole width of the cave.
sequence.voice: Among the things these books call concepts rather than realities, they list the whole made of parts, the shape, the being, the direction, the time, and then space, and for space the two examples they give are a well and a cave. A thing named by what is not in it. Somebody stood on this ledge two thousand years ago and cut a line in the stone so the rain would fall clear of the hole.

sequence.on_screen: Rain. It comes in off open country and arrives. Water pours off the lip of the overhang in an unbroken curtain in front of the cave mouth, and behind the curtain the cave is dark and entirely dry.
sequence.voice: Everything the mind takes hold of counts equally as a thing, these books say: what you hear said, what you see written or printed, what you merely think. A line on a palm leaf is a thing taken up by a mind. It lasts as long as the leaf is kept dry and somebody copies it before it goes. That is the whole mechanism by which the history of an island survived, and you are looking at the part of it that was made of rock.

sequence.on_screen: Inside a cave, working with the daylight that reaches in and no more. A reclining figure fourteen metres long. Then the walls: panelled Jātaka scenes, register above register, a strong blue running through them, and flaking where the damp has got in.
sequence.voice: Every panel on this wall is a story, and the stories are the plainer level of the same teaching, put into pictures anyone can read. It would be easy to say the beauty of it is only in whoever is looking. These books say the opposite, and they are stubborn about it: whether a thing is desirable is not set by the mind that likes or dislikes it. A mind can be delighted by what is foul and repelled by what is fine, and be wrong both times.

sequence.on_screen: Letters. A short inscription cut into the rock of a cave wall, then painted lettering on a later panel; the round, stylus-shaped script that palm leaf made necessary.
sequence.voice: The sound of a word is a real event. It arrives, it stops. The name it carries is not a thing in the same way. Say three syllables in order and a whole object stands up in the listener's mind, and the same happens through the eye, off a wall or off a leaf. These books then sort names six ways by whether the name and the thing under it are ultimately there or not. That is a technical sorting. It is not a list of true names and false ones, and nobody on this rock is using the wrong word for anything.

sequence.on_screen: The top terrace at the end of the day. Stupa, bo tree, open sky. Below, the shower that came through is crossing the lowland, the sea flat to one side, mountains to the other. Last light off the rock face.
sequence.voice: Two levels of one teaching, then, and the plainer one exists so the other can be got at. But do not let the climb stand for anything. These books say the final realities are beyond human knowing and beyond the knowing of gods, that they were reported by an omniscience nobody here claims, and nothing about standing higher up or reading more carefully brings them nearer. The plainer version was never a compromise. Rock. Rain. Leaf. Every one of those words worked perfectly today.

concept_merge.why_together: The three digests converge on one question that this rock's own history already asks: why would a teaching need a second, plainer level of itself? C001 answers it directly. The Pradeepika splits the Buddha's word into conventional teaching and ultimate teaching [C001-P:L47–L53], and says the conventional teaching keeps inside everyday names, being, person, tree, mountain, river, for a stated reason, so that each person could understand easily [C001-P:L51]. A prose commentary is that same move performed on a text: a plainer register supplied so the harder one can be followed. C084 gives the machinery. Paññatti is both what is made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25]; a name-concept is the name assigned to a reality or to a meaning-concept [C084-P:L47]; and among the meaning-concepts the sources list space, whose two examples are a well and a cave [C084-P:L27–L41], which is what a cave temple is. The Margaya then separates the spoken sound, which is ultimately real, from the name it conveys, which is not, and describes three syllables in sequence raising a whole object in the hearer's mind [C084-M:L21], and says the same arises when the thing is seen with the eye [C084-M:L9], which is what reading is. C077 supplies the register of the word itself: the compendium takes khandha only in the plain sense of heap, collection or portion and sets the grander senses of the same term aside [C077-P:L36–L42]. A text that chooses the plain sense of its own key word is doing on one word what a commentary does on a whole chronicle.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the interesting thing is not that a plain version exists, but that the plain version is load-bearing. C001 alone risks a film about doctrine; C084 alone makes a film about language; C077 alone is a classification. Together they make the rock itself the argument, because on this rock every level is provided so that another level can be reached: a stair cut up a cleft, a channel cut along a brow so rain drips clear, painted stories on a cave wall telling the hard part in pictures, and a prose commentary kept next to a verse chronicle for two thousand years because without it the verse could not be read. The pairing also closes the exit the film would otherwise take. C001's digest states that the final realities are known by omniscient knowledge rather than by human or divine knowing [C001-P:L59], so nothing about climbing higher or reading better can be offered as arriving anywhere, and C077's digest forbids the softer landing too: desirability is not simply relative to the beholder [C077-P:L193–L201], so the film cannot end on every reading being as good as any other.

concept_links.why: The Pradeepika's division of the Buddha's word into sammuti-desanā and paramattha-desanā, and its mapping of them onto two parts of the canon, is the whole spine [C001-P:L47–L53]. Its reason for the conventional register is the film's argument in one line: the teaching stayed inside everyday usage, being, person, tree, mountain, river, so that each listener could understand easily [C001-P:L51], which makes a plainer level a deliberate instrument and not a concession. The Margaya supplies what a written line is: whatever the mind takes up, through hearing words, through seeing what is written or printed, through thinking, is an attha [C001-M:L38], and most of what the world takes to be there is not ultimately there [C001-M:L40], with paññatti as the name for what is held to exist by notion alone [C001-M:L48]. Two of the digest's limits are load-bearing and are written into the sequence, not left to the risks. The film must not flatten the Margaya's blunt wording into 'nothing is real': the sources keep the ultimate realities fully real and the conventional register fully valid. And the film must not let its own climb imply progress toward the ultimate, because the Pradeepika says the final realities are a non-substantial kind of process known by omniscient knowledge and not by human or even divine knowing [C001-P:L59]; beat 8 exists to say so out loud. The digest also warns that the Margaya's own stakes, including rebirth, merit and the rightness of image worship [C001-M:L5–L17], are the source's commitments and cannot be quietly dropped or presented as observable fact, which matters in a film that goes inside working image houses.

This digest gives the film its vocabulary and one of its best images. Paññatti is defined as both what is made known and the means of making it known [C084-P:L25], and a name-concept is specifically the name assigned either to an ultimate reality or to a meaning-concept [C084-P:L47]. Among the meaning-concepts the sources list the collective whole, using earth, mountain, river and sea as examples, along with shape, being, direction, time, space and the meditation sign, and for space the examples given are a well and a cave [C084-P:L27–L41]: a cave temple is the sources' own illustration, a thing named by what is not in it. The Margaya's sound-and-name distinction is what the film can actually observe on a wall and on a leaf: the sound is ultimately real, the name it conveys is not, and three syllables heard in order raise a whole object in the hearer's mind [C084-M:L21], with the same arising when a thing is taken in by the eye [C084-M:L9]. The division test comes with it, cloth pulled apart leaving only thread [C084-M:L7], and so does the sixfold sorting of names by whether name and basis are ultimately existent [C084-P:L49–L71]. The digest's guards are absolute here and beat 7 carries them: the existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not a scheme of true and false, the sources keep conventional wholes useful and valid in their own domain, and a film must never tell a participant that the name they use is wrong, which in a living monastery includes every name used for this rock, these caves and these images.

The compendium's own choice of register is the reason it belongs here. Of the several senses the word khandha carries, the sources keep only heap, collection and portion, and explicitly set aside the others, including the virtue-group sense and the sense of a log [C077-P:L36–L42]: a text choosing the plain sense of its own key word, which is what this film is about. What the sorting is for is stated without ornament, to take apart the grasping 'this is me, this is mine' so that it can be let go [C077-P:L982–L984; C077-M:L24]. The digest also supplies a second, harder guard the film needs at exactly the point where it is most tempted to be generous: whether an object is desirable is fixed by the result-consciousness and measured by an average person, and 'cannot be deceived', even where the reacting mind likes what is foul or hates what is fine [C077-P:L193–L201]. That is the reverse of 'beauty is in the eye of the beholder', and beat 6 says so over the painted walls rather than letting the film drift into every reading being as good as another. Two further limits travel with it. The analysis is not the claim that nobody exists, and it is not a model of personality. And the inferior-and-superior aspect runs through a rebirth cosmology and a pre-modern social order [C077-P:L203–L207] and must never be read onto the monastery, its occupants, its visitors or the relative standing of the terraces.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a plainer version of something is not always a watering-down, and can be the only reason the harder thing survives at all. The proof needs no doctrine and no vocabulary: a groove cut in rock so the rain falls clear of a cave, painted stories on the wall inside it, and a prose commentary kept beside a verse chronicle for two thousand years because without it nobody could read the verse.
what_must_be_real: This is a working monastery, not a monument, and the floor applies in full. No monk is presented as attained, composed, wise or serene, and no monk is a figure in the film's argument; a camera cannot show what is in anyone's mind and this film does not pretend otherwise. Nobody is an exhibit, and nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera is filmed. No act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repositioned or lit for filming, and no observance is staged or asked for. No manuscript is handled, opened, unwrapped or carried for the camera unless those responsible for it freely offer, and if the offer is not made the film says on screen that the leaves were not filmed rather than substituting something that looks like them. The paintings are filmed in the light that is there; nothing is cleaned, wetted, touched or relit, and the flaking is shown as it is rather than framed as neglect. The rain is whatever rain arrives, never simulated, composited or graded into existence. The historical record is stated as recorded and no further: the film does not narrate the 1826 transaction as a gift of understanding to the island and does not narrate it as a theft, because the sources do not settle it.
position_hint: middle to late in the group: it is the film that explains why the group's whole method of everyday names exists, so it wants at least two films of simpler naming behind it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Becoming a film about books and manuscripts. The subject is a rock, its terraces, its caves and its weather; the text is what the voice explains over them, and if the cut can only be held together by close-ups of palm leaf the film has failed.
The colonial layer narrated as a gift of understanding to the island, or narrated as theft. What happened is recorded; what it was is disputed and stays disputed, on screen and in narration.

Any implication that the island's history began when a European read it. The chronicle, its commentary and the monastery that kept them all long predate 1826 and the film says so before it says his name.

Presenting a monk as composed, wise or attained, or letting a robe in frame carry the voice's authority. The digests say a camera cannot show which mental factor is present and the series' floor forbids it outright.
Filming worship as spectacle, or treating an observance as an interesting custom. The monastery is in use and the film has no claim on any of it.
Flattening the Margaya's blunt 'does not truly exist' into 'nothing is real'; the sources keep sound, colour, feeling and mind fully real and treat conventional wholes as valid in their own domain.

Letting the climb and the terraces imply spiritual progress or arrival. The Pradeepika says the final realities are known by omniscient knowledge and not by human or divine knowing [C001-P:L59], and beat 8 exists to refuse the reading the geography invites.

The softer error in the other direction: 'every reading is as good as another', which the C077 digest contradicts head-on, since desirability is not simply relative to the beholder [C077-P:L193–L201].
Treating the sources' existent and non-existent pairs as true and false names, or suggesting to anyone here that a name they use for the rock, a cave or an image is a mistake.

Quietly dropping or naturalising the Margaya's own commitments, which in this extract include rebirth, merit and demerit and the rightness of image worship [C001-M:L5–L17]. They are the source's stakes, not observable facts, and a film shot inside image houses must neither endorse them as evidence nor edit them out.
Reading the sources' inferior-and-superior ladder onto the terraces, the monastery or anybody on it; it belongs to a rebirth cosmology and a pre-modern social order [C077-P:L203–L207].

Archetype overlap with the group and slate: this is the second rock-temple location proposed across the slate and the other one also turns on a text kept at a monastery. The two films have to differ in the frame, the weather and the concept, or one of them goes.
Drone flight over a working religious site above people on narrow terraces, which may be refused outright and should be assumed refused until it is not.
drop_if: Filming cannot happen without interrupting worship or crowding the terraces and the stair.
The film can only be made by having a manuscript brought out, opened or handled for the camera.
No rain can be obtained in the window available, so the central shot of water pouring off a cave brow onto a dry interior does not exist.
The colonial layer cannot be stated as recorded without the monastery, or anyone else, being asked to endorse one reading of it.

connections.note: The confirmed opening film shows many names doing their work on one mountain; this one shows why a second, plainer level of a teaching had to exist at all. Both rest on the Pradeepika's line that everyday names were the deliberate method.
Cloth pulled back to thread, and a chronicle pulled back to the prose that makes it readable: the same test on a fabric and on a text.
The sources' two examples of a space-concept are a well and a cave. One film takes the well, this one takes the cave.

selection.reason: A landmark whose recorded history is the concept's own question: a verse chronicle that could not be read until a prose commentary kept beside it was found, on a rock that supplies terraces, painted caves and one extraordinary weather shot.

review.note: Rewritten onto a new location after the hand-dug moonstone pits were set aside. The title is kept and the concept set is unchanged, but the body is new throughout and the old gem-washing film is gone, including its division-of-ground spine and its payoff shot. The location is now a terraced rock temple in the southern lowlands, named only inside suggested_location, and the film is built on its verified history rather than on an analogy: in 1826 George Turnour, a British civil servant, obtained at this monastery's library palm-leaf copies of the tika, the prose commentary on the Mahāvaṃsa, whose verse had been effectively unreadable; a monk told him a prose key existed, and fitted to the verse it 'reduces it to a commonsense narrative'. That commentary produced the first English translation in 1837 and with it the island's recoverable chronology. The island's recorded history survived as palm leaves kept dry in a cave library in the wet south, and was legible only because a second, plainer text had been kept beside it. That is exactly C001's Pradeepika claim performed on a text: the Buddha taught in everyday names, being, person, tree, mountain, river, so that listeners could understand easily, so a plainer register is a deliberate instrument rather than a concession. C084 was re-grounded on the sources' own example of a space-concept, a well and a cave, plus the sound-and-name distinction and the sixfold sorting of names; C077 was re-grounded on the compendium's choice of the plain sense of khandha over the grander senses of the same word, and on its guard that desirability is not simply relative to the beholder, which beat 6 now carries. Every citation was re-checked against the digest evidence. The living-monastery floor, the no-manuscript-handling condition and the refusal to narrate the colonial transaction as either gift or theft are written into what_must_be_real, the risks and the historical thread rather than left implicit. A new historical_thread block records the story, the binding, and what is certain as against what is disputed, including the 1826-or-1827 date, whether Turnour found the leaves or was given transcriptions, and the rock's height. Eight Commons images verified to exist.

suggested_location.region: Hambantota District, Southern Province, inland of Tangalle in the lowland country north of the coast road
suggested_location.why_here: Because the history of this rock asks the concept's question before the film opens its mouth. The island's recorded chronology exists in English because a verse chronicle that nobody could read was matched, in 1826, with a prose commentary that had been kept on palm leaf in the library of this monastery; the plainer text was not a study aid but the condition of the harder text being legible at all. That is C001's own claim about conventional teaching, performed on a document, and it happened here. The rock then supplies the cinema the argument needs in the same frames. It stands a little over two hundred metres out of flat country, so it can be established from the air as one mass with four lesser rocks around it. Its caves are the sources' literal example of a space-concept, a thing named by what is not in it, and they are cut across five stepped terraces reached by a stone stair through a natural cleft, so the film's structure is the site's. And along the brow above every cave mouth there is a hand-cut channel whose entire purpose is to make rain drip clear of the opening, which hands the film its best and clearest shot at once: a curtain of monsoon water pouring off the lip of an overhang with the cave behind it dark and dry. The thing that kept the manuscripts readable is a groove in a rock, and it is photographable. No other candidate gives the history and that shot in the same place.
what_to_film: The rock from the air at first light, wide enough to hold the flat lowland, the mist in it and the four smaller rocks standing off the main mass. This is the establishing frame and it wants a still morning.
The stone stair up through the natural cleft: a few hundred steps, the tree roots crossing them, and the light dropping as the walls close in. Filmed from the steps at head height, not from above.
The terraces from the air but tight and looking along the face rather than down, in raked morning or late light, so the five stacked levels and the cave mouths on each read as one structure.
One cave mouth in full from the terrace outside it, with the overhang above and the hand-cut channel along its brow held long enough to be read as man-made and deliberate.

The rain: water pouring off the lip of an overhang in an unbroken curtain in front of a cave mouth, with the dry dark interior behind it. This is the payoff and everything else is built to be there when it happens.

Inside a cave, in the daylight that reaches in and no more: a reclining figure at full length, then the painted walls panel by panel, including the flaking, and the strong blue that distinguishes the southern work.
Letters: a short inscription cut into the rock of a cave wall, and painted lettering on a later panel, both filmed as marks in a surface rather than as documents.
The top terrace at either end of the day: stupa, bo tree, open sky, and the 360-degree ground below it, with a shower crossing the lowland if one can be caught from up there.
Weather from the air at a distance: a shower coming in across open country toward the rock, which is the shot that sets up the rain sequence.
suggested_location.access: By road inland from the coast at Tangalle, roughly twenty kilometres, on a made road to the foot of the rock; there is a site museum and a ticket arrangement at the bottom. Above that it is on foot only, up a stone stair of a few hundred steps through the cleft, with the terraces linked by further steps. It is a living monastery with resident monks and daily worship, so access above the lower terrace is a matter of permission from those responsible for the site rather than of a ticket, and that permission governs the caves, the paintings, the museum's manuscript holdings and anything approaching the library. Drone flight over a working religious site and over people on narrow terraces must be assumed refused until it is specifically granted. Carrying gear up a wet stone stair is its own constraint on what can be attempted in rain.
suggested_location.best_time: Early morning for the rock out of the mist and for light reaching into the lower caves; late afternoon for raked light on the terraces; either end of the day at the summit. The film needs showers, so the wet windows rather than the dry: broadly the second inter-monsoon in October and November, and again around the onset of the south-west monsoon in May. A week with both showery and clear mornings is what the shot list actually wants, and the rain shot cannot be scheduled.

suggested_location.research_note: Coordinates, the 205 m rock height, the four surrounding rocks, the five terraced compounds and seven cave temples, the stair of roughly 533 steps through a natural cleft, the Kandyan-era paintings and their named Jātaka subjects, the reclining figures at fourteen to fifteen metres, the three dated inscriptions from the second-to-first centuries BC, the sixth-to-seventh centuries AD and the ninth-to-tenth centuries AD, the bo tree held to be one of the thirty-two saplings, the Dutch name, the site museum with palm-leaf holdings, and the Turnour episode are all desk research from the sources above. Two things I could not settle and have recorded as disputed rather than smoothing: the height (205 m in one source, 180 m in another, 'over 200 m' in a third) and the year (1826 in most accounts, 1827 in one). The wet and dry windows are general regional climatology and not site observation. The drip-ledge channels above the cave mouths are standard for drip-ledged cave monasteries in Sri Lanka and are reported for this site's caves, but I have not confirmed from a photograph which specific cave mouths here carry a visible cut channel, and the film's central shot depends on it. Access above the lower terrace, permission for interiors, whether any manuscript could be filmed, current painting condition, and drone rules over a working religious site are all unverified.

historical_thread.story: The rock has been monastic ground for well over two thousand years. Early Brahmi inscriptions of the second and first centuries BC record cave donations by monks named Culatissa and Upasona; the foundation is attributed to King Saddhatissa, and later patronage to kings including Datusena and, in the eighteenth century, Kirti Sri Rajasinha, whose period the surviving paintings mostly belong to. Medieval inscriptions call the place Muhudugiri, the sea rock, Pali Samudda-giri. Seven cave temples are cut back under the rock's overhangs on five stepped terraces reached by a stone stair of some five hundred steps through a natural cleft, and the caves hold reclining figures up to about fifteen metres long and walls painted in layers laid over one another across three or four centuries. Eighteenth-century Dutch visitors called the rock Adam's Berg, confusing it with the peak in the highlands. In 1826 George Turnour, a British civil servant in the Ceylon Civil Service, obtained at this monastery's library palm-leaf copies of the tika, the prose commentary on the Mahāvaṃsa, later known as the Vaṃsatthappakāsinī. The chronicle's Pali verse had been effectively unreadable to European scholarship, which had treated it as ornamental poetry rather than record. A monk, named in the nineteenth-century accounts as Gallé, told Turnour that a prose key existed and was convinced the chronicle was an accurate record buried under metrical rhetoric; Turnour's own description of a tika is a prose key which, fitted into the mystical verse of the earlier poets, reduces it to a commonsense narrative. Working from it he produced the first printed edition and English translation of the Mahāvaṃsa, covering thirty-eight chapters, published in 1837; Louis Corneille Wijesinha completed the remaining chapters in 1889, and Wilhelm Geiger's translation followed in 1912. The recoverable chronology of the island's recorded history rests on that chain. The material fact underneath it is unglamorous: the leaves survived because they were kept dry in cave rooms under overhangs whose brows had been grooved so that rain drips clear, in a part of the island that gets two wet seasons a year, and because each copy was recopied before it failed.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: The Pradeepika says the Buddha's word divides into conventional teaching and ultimate teaching, and that the conventional teaching deliberately stayed inside everyday names, being, person, tree, mountain, river, so that each person could understand easily [C001-P:L47–L53; C001-P:L51]. A commentary is that move performed on a text: a second, plainer level of speech supplied so that the first can be followed. That is not an analogy applied to this rock. It is what happened on it, in 1826, as a matter of record: a chronicle in verse that could not be read, a prose commentary kept beside it for centuries, and a whole recoverable history that existed only because somebody had kept the plainer version. The site then supplies the same structure physically at every scale, which is what makes it filmable rather than merely arguable: a stair cut through a cleft so that the terraces can be reached, a channel cut along a brow so that what is inside stays legible, painted panels telling the difficult part of a teaching in everyday pictures, and cave rooms which are the sources' own example of a thing named by what is not in it [C084-P:L27–L41]. The binding also brings its own limits. Nothing here is offered as arriving at the ultimate: the Pradeepika places the final realities beyond human and even divine knowing [C001-P:L59], so the climb cannot stand for progress. And the film does not settle whose gain 1826 was, because the record does not.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: That this is a cave monastery of great antiquity with dated inscriptions from the second and first centuries BC onward, on a rock of roughly two hundred metres, with cave temples and paintings on stepped terraces. That the Mahāvaṃsa is a Pali verse chronicle and that a prose commentary on it, the tika, exists. That George Turnour, a British civil servant in Ceylon, obtained palm-leaf manuscripts of that commentary at this monastery in the mid-1820s, that he described a tika as a prose key which fitted into the verse reduces it to a commonsense narrative, and that the first printed edition and English translation of the Mahāvaṃsa, thirty-eight chapters, was published under his name in 1837 and was made possible by the commentary. That the translation and the chronology drawn from it became the framework for the island's recorded history in European and later in Sri Lankan scholarship. That the Dutch called the rock Adam's Berg.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed: The year: 1826 in most accounts, 1827 in at least one. The transaction: accounts variously say Turnour discovered the manuscripts, found them in one of the caves, was helped to them by a monk, or received transcriptions prepared for him by the chief monk, and the difference matters because it is the difference between a find and a gift. The monk: the nineteenth-century accounts give a name, Gallé, but not a form that can be confidently reconstructed. The publication year: 1837 in most sources, 1836 in one. The rock's height: 205 m, 180 m and 'over 200 m' all appear. The number of terraces: five compounds in one account, three platforms in another, with seven cave temples in both. What it means that the island's chronology reached print through a colonial official's hands is argued about and this film does not adjudicate it; it records what happened and leaves the argument standing.

unknowns: No permission, contact or access has been obtained. Everything here is a research direction and the monastery has not been approached.
Whether any cave mouth on this rock shows a visible hand-cut drip channel that reads on camera is unconfirmed, and the film's central shot depends on it.
Whether interiors, paintings and the museum's palm-leaf holdings can be filmed at all, and on what conditions, is unknown.
